subtitle: Deaf Minnesotans form a cultural and linguistic community. Learn to tell apart Deaf, DeafBlind and hard-of-hearing experiences and to arrange communication access that meets your ADA duties.
audience: For all DHS and DSD employees, including case managers, program and policy staff, supervisors, HR partners and communications staff, who communicate with Deaf, DeafBlind or hard-of-hearing people as clients, colleagues or community partners.

lessons.title: Deaf as a culture and ASL as a language
objectives: Distinguish Deaf as a cultural and linguistic identity from deaf as an audiological description.
Explain why American Sign Language is a complete language with its own grammar, not a code for English.
Identify terms that many Deaf people find outdated or offensive.
Explain why written English may not be an accessible substitute for ASL.
lessons.teaching:
The National Association of the Deaf explains a distinction that shapes this whole course. Written with a lowercase d, deaf describes the audiological condition of not hearing. In the United States, capital-D Deaf often describes a cultural identity connected with ASL and Deaf community life. Identity is personal; neither a hearing level nor a language preference tells you how someone identifies. Deaf culture has its own history, arts, humor, values, social norms and institutions. Many Deaf people see themselves first as members of a linguistic minority, not as people defined by a hearing loss.

The National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders describes ASL as a complete, natural language with the same linguistic properties as spoken languages and a grammar that differs from English. ASL uses the hands, face and body, and has its own rules for pronunciation, word formation and word order. It has regional accents and dialects. It is not universal: British Sign Language, for example, is a different language, and signers of one cannot necessarily understand the other. Its exact origins are uncertain; researchers trace influences from local sign languages and French Sign Language more than two centuries ago. Fingerspelling is used for names and some English words, but it is a small part of the language.

This has a practical consequence that is easy to miss. For many Deaf people, ASL is their first or strongest language and English is a second language. Handing someone a written notice, or offering to pass notes, may not be effective communication for a person whose primary language is ASL, especially for complex topics like eligibility, services or rights. The reverse is also true: some deaf people do not know ASL and rely on written English, captioning or speech reading.

Language about deafness matters. The NAD notes that most people in the community reject the term hearing impaired because it focuses on what people cannot do, and considers terms like deaf and dumb or deaf-mute offensive. Deaf, DeafBlind and hard of hearing are widely accepted. The NAD's core advice is simple: when in doubt, ask the person how they identify.
lessons.keyPoint: Deaf with a capital D names a cultural and linguistic community whose language, ASL, is a full language distinct from English. Ask people how they identify and how they communicate best.
lessons.example: Practice case: Maria, a DSD communications specialist, is preparing a public notice about changes to a waiver program. A colleague suggests that Deaf readers will be fine with the written English version, so an ASL video is unnecessary. Maria knows some Deaf community members use written English well, but she has heard from a Deaf advisory group member, Brian, that many people want ASL versions of important notices. The notice explains appeal rights.
lessons.question: What should Maria do?
choices: Publish only the written notice, since anyone who reads English can understand it.
Publish the written notice with an ASL video version, captions, and a plain-language summary, and ask the Deaf advisory group for feedback on the video.
Add a line to the notice telling Deaf readers to ask a family member to explain it.
feedback: For many Deaf people, English is a second language, and appeal rights are complex. A written notice alone may not provide effective communication.

This is the strongest choice. Use qualified ASL translation and accessibility review, with community feedback to improve usability. Feedback alone does not establish legal compliance. Coordinate publication so people receive accessible appeal information in time to exercise their rights.
Directing people to family members shifts the agency's responsibility onto them and may compromise privacy and accuracy.
lessons.reflection: Before this lesson, how did you think about the relationship between ASL and English? What, if anything, has changed?
lessons.action: Identify one high-stakes public document in your area, such as a notice of rights. Find out whether an ASL version exists and, if not, raise the gap with the document owner or your division's communications lead.

check.question: Which statement about American Sign Language is accurate?
check.correct: ASL is a complete natural language with its own grammar that differs from English.
wrong: ASL is English expressed word for word with the hands.
ASL is a universal sign language used by Deaf people worldwide.
check.feedback: ASL has its own grammar, word order and regional variation, and it is not universal. Treating it as signed English or as universal leads to poor communication choices.

lessons.title: Deaf, DeafBlind, hard of hearing and late deafened
objectives: Distinguish Deaf, DeafBlind, hard-of-hearing and late-deafened experiences and communication needs.
Identify communication options, including ASL interpreting, tactile interpreting, captioning and assistive listening.
Explain why one in five Minnesotans with hearing loss is not one group with one need.
Plan a question that lets a person name the communication method that works for them.
lessons.teaching:
DHS Deaf, DeafBlind and Hard of Hearing State Services notes that one in five Minnesotans has a hearing loss. The Commission uses the same estimate, which covers varied hearing experiences and does not measure membership in Deaf culture.

Deaf people who use ASL as their primary language usually need a qualified ASL interpreter, ASL video content, or a signing staff member who is fluent enough for the conversation. Hard-of-hearing people have varied hearing levels and communication preferences. Many use hearing aids or cochlear implants, captioning, assistive listening systems or speech reading, and many do not use ASL. The NAD notes that some hard-of-hearing people describe themselves as in some ways hearing and in some ways deaf. Late-deafened people lost their hearing as adults, often after a lifetime in spoken English. Some use real-time captioning or written communication. Do not assume a person’s emotional response, language background or preferred method.

DeafBlind people have combined hearing and vision loss. Communication varies widely, including tactile signing when the person chooses this method. Ask before initiating touch or arranging physical guidance. Others use close-vision signing, braille, large print, or amplification combined with magnification. The ADA lists tactile interpreters among the auxiliary aids that may be required. DeafBlind people may also need support persons for navigating spaces, and DHS State Services offers programs specifically for people with combined vision and hearing loss.

Because the range is so wide, the best starting point is a question, not a guess. How do you prefer to communicate? What works best for you in meetings, on the phone, and in writing? Is there anything that makes communication harder, such as lighting, background noise or group conversations? Record relevant preferences only in the authorized system, with access limited to the service purpose. Confirm them when circumstances change. Keep in mind that preferences can differ by setting: someone may be fine with captions in a large webinar but need an interpreter for a one-on-one conversation about services. Give primary consideration to the person's requested aid in public services. Convenience alone does not justify a different method; it must meet the effective-communication requirements explained in lesson four.
lessons.keyPoint: Hearing loss covers many experiences. Deaf ASL users, hard-of-hearing people, late-deafened adults and DeafBlind people often need different kinds of access, so ask each person what works.
lessons.example: Practice case: Harold, a man in his seventies, lost his hearing over the past few years. He is meeting with a county worker, Ruth, about in-home supports. The county has booked an ASL interpreter because his file says deaf. When they arrive, Harold says he does not know sign language and asks whether they can use captions on a laptop instead. Ruth is not sure the county has a captioning option ready. For now, Ruth needs only to confirm arrangements, not conduct the assessment. Harold confirms that the county-approved typing tool works for this short exchange; no sensitive assessment details will be entered. Ruth can arrange qualified real-time captioning before discussing services.
lessons.question: What should Ruth do?
choices: Continue with the ASL interpreter, since one was already booked and paid for.
Communicate by passing handwritten notes for the whole assessment.
Use whatever quick captioning or typing option is available for now, confirm Harold's preference, and arrange real-time captioning for future meetings, updating the file.
feedback: An ASL interpreter does not help someone who does not know ASL. The booked service does not create effective communication.
Notes may work for a short exchange, but an in-depth assessment through handwritten notes is slow and may lose detail. It should not be the plan for future meetings.

This is the strongest choice in this short scheduling exchange. Confirm that the approved tool works for Harold and record his preference in the authorized system. Do not begin the substantive assessment unless communication is effective; arrange qualified captioning and protect service deadlines. An available automated tool is not automatically an adequate substitute for CART.
lessons.reflection: How does your team currently learn a person's communication preference before a meeting? Where could that information get lost?
lessons.action: Find out how your unit arranges real-time captioning, sometimes called CART, as well as ASL and tactile interpreting. Save the steps and lead times in a place your team uses.

check.question: A file says a person is deaf. What is the best way to plan communication access for the next meeting?
check.correct: Ask the person which method works for them, since they may use ASL, captioning, assistive listening, tactile interpreting or another method.
wrong: Book an ASL interpreter, since all deaf people use ASL.
Plan to communicate in writing, since all deaf people read English.
check.feedback: A label does not establish a communication method. Ask the person, confirm what works for the setting, and record only relevant preferences in the authorized system.

lessons.title: Deaf Minnesota: history and institutions
objectives: Summarize the history of the Minnesota State Academy for the Deaf and its role in Deaf community life.
Describe the role of the Minnesota Commission of the Deaf, DeafBlind and Hard of Hearing.
Identify services offered by DHS Deaf, DeafBlind and Hard of Hearing State Services.
Plan how to involve Deaf-led organizations in DHS work.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota's Deaf community has deep roots. At its first legislative session after statehood, a representative from Faribault proposed a school for deaf children. The Civil War delayed the plan, but the legislature authorized the school in 1863, and it opened in rented rooms in Faribault that September. Its first superintendent came from the Ohio School for the Deaf. Now called the Minnesota State Academy for the Deaf, it still operates in Faribault, preparing deaf and hard-of-hearing students from across the state to reach their fullest potential.

This history provides context for learning about Minnesota’s Deaf community; it does not describe every person’s school experience. Ask about relevant experiences only when the person chooses to share them. Avoid assuming that someone attended the academy, uses ASL, or belongs to the same organizations as another Deaf Minnesotan.

The Minnesota Commission of the Deaf, DeafBlind and Hard of Hearing is a state agency that advocates for communication access and equal opportunity for the twenty percent of Minnesotans who are deaf, DeafBlind or hard of hearing. It works on issues in education, employment, health care, civic engagement and communication access, and pursues a legislative agenda. It is an advocacy body, not a direct service provider.

Within DHS, Deaf, DeafBlind and Hard of Hearing State Services works through regional offices around the state. It offers consultation and referral, the Minnesota Access to Communication Technology program, which provides eligible people with communication equipment, programs for people with combined hearing and vision loss, and mental health therapy with ASL-fluent professionals. Its grants support services such as interpreter referral, mentoring, local-news captioning and DeafBlind support. Check current eligibility and availability before promising a service. For DHS staff, these offices are colleagues and resources. Before designing a program change, engagement effort or public message that affects Deaf, DeafBlind or hard-of-hearing Minnesotans, consult State Services and invite Deaf-led organizations to help shape it.
lessons.keyPoint: Minnesota’s Deaf community includes long-established institutions and varied individual experiences. The Commission advocates for access, while DHS State Services provides services and expertise. Involve relevant partners early when planning work that affects these communities.
lessons.example: Practice case: Tom, a DSD project lead, is planning a statewide survey about service experiences. The plan calls for an online English survey and phone follow-ups. A team member, Keisha, asks whether Deaf and DeafBlind Minnesotans have been considered. Tom says the survey is short and anyone can type answers. The survey launches in six weeks, and the team has not contacted anyone outside DSD.
lessons.question: What should Tom do?
choices: Consult DHS Deaf, DeafBlind and Hard of Hearing State Services and Deaf-led organizations now, and add ASL video versions, accessible formats and alternatives to phone follow-up.
Launch the survey as planned and handle access requests if anyone asks.
Exclude the phone follow-up for everyone so no one is disadvantaged.
feedback: This is the strongest choice. It uses the expertise already inside DHS, involves the community before launch, and builds access into the design instead of adding it later.
Waiting for requests puts the burden on the people facing barriers, and many will simply not take part. The results would then undercount their experiences.
Removing follow-up for everyone reduces the survey's value and does not address the English-only design. Access means adding workable options, not removing features.
lessons.reflection: Which offices and community organizations do you usually consult early in a project? Who is missing from that list?
lessons.action: Find the regional DHS Deaf, DeafBlind and Hard of Hearing State Services office that serves your area and add its contact to your project planning checklist.

check.question: Which statement best describes the Minnesota Commission of the Deaf, DeafBlind and Hard of Hearing?
check.correct: A state agency that advocates for communication access and equal opportunity through policy and legislation.
wrong: The DHS unit that provides telephone equipment and mental health therapy.
A private company that employs interpreters.
check.feedback: The Commission advocates and pursues policy change. Direct services such as telephone equipment and ASL-fluent mental health therapy come from DHS Deaf, DeafBlind and Hard of Hearing State Services. Knowing the difference helps you reach the right partner.

lessons.title: Communication access in practice: ADA duties and interpreters
objectives: Explain the ADA's effective communication requirements for state agencies, including primary consideration.
Identify what makes an interpreter qualified and when family members may not interpret.
Describe when a Deaf interpreter or Certified Deaf Interpreter may be needed.
Plan an interpreter request that avoids common mistakes.
lessons.teaching:
As a state agency, DHS is covered by Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act, which requires effective communication with people who have communication disabilities. The ADA lists auxiliary aids and services such as qualified sign language, oral, cued-speech and tactile interpreters, real-time captioning, written materials and video phones. State and local governments must give primary consideration to the aid or service the person asks for. They may use a different option only if it would be equally effective, or if the request would cause an undue burden or fundamentally alter the program, under the formal process in 28 CFR 35.164. The head of the public entity or a designated decision-maker must consider all available program resources and give written reasons for a burden or fundamental-alteration finding. Staff should involve the ADA coordinator, but that role alone does not confer decision authority. The agency must still take other available steps to provide access to the maximum extent possible. People are not charged for these aids.

The ADA defines a qualified interpreter as one who can interpret effectively, accurately and impartially, both receptively and expressively, using any necessary specialized vocabulary. Knowing some sign language is not enough. Agencies may not require people to bring their own interpreter. An accompanying adult or minor child may interpret in an emergency involving an imminent safety or welfare threat when no interpreter is available. Outside that narrow exception, a child may not interpret. An accompanying adult may do so only at the person’s specific request, with the adult’s agreement, when reliance is appropriate. Conflicts of interest or ineffective communication rule out that option. If video remote interpreting is used, it must meet quality standards, including uninterrupted full-motion video, images large and clear enough to show both signers’ faces and hands, clear audio, and trained staff. Technical compliance alone is insufficient if the person cannot use it effectively; arrange an effective alternative.

Sometimes the best team includes a Deaf interpreter. The Minnesota Commission of the Deaf, DeafBlind and Hard of Hearing explains that Deaf interpreters are fluent in ASL and English and bring native sign choices, facial expression and cultural knowledge. They often team with hearing interpreters. They can be especially helpful for Deaf people with limited language, people who use a different sign language, DeafBlind people who use tactile signing, and high-stakes settings. Certified Deaf Interpreters hold national certification. The cited Commission article dates from 2020; its workforce counts are not a current availability estimate. Match the interpreter’s skills to the individual, language and setting rather than assuming certification alone establishes suitability.

A good interpreter request covers the basics: the person's preferred method, the setting and topic, how long the meeting will run, whether team interpreting or a Deaf interpreter is needed, and any materials the interpreter should review. During the meeting, speak directly to the Deaf person, not to the interpreter, and allow time for interpretation. If you are unsure what the law requires, or a request seems difficult to meet, contact your ADA coordinator rather than deciding on your own.

These Title II rules concern public programs and services. Employee accommodation requests also follow the employment accommodation process; involve HR and the designated accommodation staff when a colleague needs workplace access.
lessons.keyPoint: Effective communication is a legal duty. Give primary consideration to the person's choice, use qualified interpreters, including Deaf interpreters when needed, and send hard questions to the ADA coordinator.
lessons.example: Practice case: Luis, a Deaf man who uses ASL, has an appeal conference about a service reduction. The DHS staff member, Carol, has trouble booking an in-person interpreter and suggests that Luis's hearing sister, who signs, interpret instead. Luis says he would prefer a professional interpreter and has had trouble understanding video interpreting on small screens. The conference is in five days.
lessons.question: What should Carol do?
choices: Proceed with the sister, since she signs and Luis knows her.
Book video remote interpreting on the standard office laptop, since it is the fastest option.
Keep working to book a qualified in-person interpreter, consider a short postponement if needed, and consult the ADA coordinator if an equally effective option must be considered.
feedback: Luis has asked for a professional interpreter. Using a relative in an appeal about his own services raises accuracy, impartiality and privacy concerns and does not meet his request.
Luis has said video interpreting on small screens has not worked for him. Using it without meeting quality standards and without considering his preference may not be effective communication.

This is the strongest choice. Continue arranging effective access and involve the ADA coordinator promptly. Any postponement must be coordinated with the hearing authority and protect appeal deadlines, rights and service continuity; it is not permission to delay an appeal unilaterally.
lessons.reflection: When access is hard to arrange quickly, what pressures push toward shortcuts? How could your team plan to reduce them?
lessons.action: Write a short interpreter request template for your team that includes preferred method, setting, topic, length, need for team or Deaf interpreters, and materials to share. Ask your ADA coordinator or accessibility lead to review it.

check.question: Under Title II of the ADA, what must a state agency do when a Deaf person requests a particular communication aid?
check.correct: Give primary consideration to the requested aid, using another option only if it is equally effective or the request would cause an undue burden or fundamental alteration, as determined by the responsible officials.
wrong: Provide whatever aid is cheapest, as long as some aid is offered.
Ask the person to bring a family member to interpret.
check.feedback: Give primary consideration to the requested aid and establish that any alternative is equally effective. A burden or fundamental-alteration determination requires the public entity’s head or designee, consideration of all available program resources, and written reasons. Involve the ADA coordinator without assuming that role alone has this authority.

cards.back: In the United States, a cultural identity often connected with ASL and Deaf community life. Ask each person how they identify; language and hearing level do not establish identity.
A complete natural language with its own grammar, distinct from English and not universal.
Combined hearing and vision loss. Communication may include tactile or close-vision signing, braille, large print or amplification.
Under ADA Title II, state and local governments must give primary consideration to the communication aid a person requests.
A Deaf interpreter fluent in ASL and English who often teams with a hearing interpreter. Certified Deaf Interpreters hold national certification.

aid.heading: Ask and record
items: Ask how the person prefers to communicate: ASL, captioning, assistive listening, tactile or another method.
Ask how they identify, and use that term.
Record relevant preferences in the authorized system, limit access to the service purpose, and confirm them when circumstances change.
Check whether needs differ by setting, such as webinars versus one-on-one meetings.

aid.heading: Arrange access
items: Book qualified interpreters or captioners early, with topic, length and materials.
Ask about language and access needs when considering a Deaf interpreter; match the person and setting rather than assuming one arrangement fits everyone.
Do not require a person to bring an interpreter. Children may interpret only during an imminent-threat emergency when no interpreter is available.
Use video remote interpreting only if it meets quality standards and suits the person.

aid.heading: Partners and escalation
items: Consult DHS Deaf, DeafBlind and Hard of Hearing State Services early in projects.
Invite Deaf-led organizations and the Commission's guidance when shaping policy or outreach.
Provide ASL versions of important public notices.
Involve the ADA coordinator; formal burden findings require the public entity’s head or designee and written reasons.
